correctness.rationale: In the ten-vertex graph of unordered nonmerged pairs plus a merged sink, the distance from a pair to the sink is its shortest merging word length. A shortest path cannot repeat a nonmerged pair, so its length is at most ten if finite. If all pairs can merge, successively merging any pair in the current image strictly reduces its size until a reset word has been built; the converse is immediate. A separately authored computation exhausted all 9,765,625 ordered map pairs with forward shortest-distance layers. It reproduced counts 31225, 1852520, 3544680, 1798320, 613920, 175440, 38160, 7440, 1440, 240 at radii 1 through 10, respectively; 1702240 infinite; and weighted finite sum 26027825 over 8063385, giving mean 5205565/1612677. The entire set of 240 radius-ten transition pairs equals the orbit generated from the displayed Černý representative by all state relabelings and both letter orders. Its ten pair distances and the ten-step word agree with the frozen proof.
residual_risks: This is exhaustive for complete deterministic automata with five labeled states and two distinguished letters only. The radius does not measure the shortest word resetting all five states simultaneously.

value.rationale: The distance of the hardest prescribed pair is a natural measure of pair compression, finer in a different direction than the available reset-length or max–min censuses. The complete five-state binary distribution quantifies how rare slow pairs are, and the exact orbit equality gives the sharp statement that attainment of the general bound is confined to the classical example at this order. This addresses that concrete finite classification, not merely a rediscovery of the upper bound or witness.
residual_risks: No larger-order uniqueness conjecture, reset-time law, or general census algorithm improvement is claimed.
